I find it less confusing to use the "current industry standard"
point system as apparently endorsed by LSJ:

Inferior: 1 point
Superior: 2 point
Title: 0.5 points per vote. (Bishop/Primogen = 0.5,
Prince/Archbishop/Priscus/2
votes = 1, Cardinal/Justicar = 1.5, IC = 2).
+1 bleed or +1 hand damage = 1 point
Weird specials: Typically 1 or 2 points. Corner-case specials are often
free.

Points:
1-4 caps: Capacity - 1
5-6 caps: Capacity
7-8 caps: Capacity + 1
9-10 caps: Capacity + 2

So Carna, with 3 superiors, has 6 points of disciplines, 1
point for the +1 intercept, 0.5 point for being primogen,
and apparently about 0.5 point for the "eat a retainer"
special. 8 points for a 7 cap is the current standard, so
there you go.

Check Jost Werner for a comparable example: 2 superiors =
4 points, 1 inferior = 1 point, +1 stealth = 1 point -> 6
points for a 6-cap.

Josh

>combination to, and whether the disciplines are themselves good
>(individually and as a team).

The reason inclan disciplines are better* is precisely because there are more
vampires with those combinations of disciplines. Being able to fill out a
crypt (minimizing duplication when possible) is important to a deck working.

* On average. A point system can't accurately take in every individual
difference between vampires and still be useful as a design guideline.

While I agree that the very existence of in clan disciplines makes it
easier to focus a deck for a certain task, conversely, it would impose
limitations on the same set of vampires precisely because they focus
so strongly in only 3 areas.

I'm not sure if it's just because people are creative, get bored or
want to splice some "good stuff" together, but people do seek out
interesting combinations to play. It doesn't take much effort to look
through the TWD list and find a healthy number of decks winning
tournaments that don't just splash an extra clan (I'd say two clans of
4+ vampires is the threshhold here. To me, this means you're serious
enough to really want one of each clan in your opening crypt.)

Anyway, for this reason I would consider out of clan disciplines to be
rated on par with in clan. The only exception I'd make is low-cap
vampires which a significant portion of out of clan disciplines--which
could be considered a liability.

Jeff

Point system is not going to be able to accurately gauge each and every
situation. The valuations of various features of vampires is an average
valuation for a feature. On average, out of clan disciplines, with the
exception of Dominate and possibly Presence, are worth significantly less than
in clan disciplines.

A point system is not the way to tell how good a vampire is. A point system
that correlates strongly with the strength of vampires as determined from
experience is a good one to use as a design guideline. I've run the numbers
using my system for every vampire through SW. Perfect? Hardly. But, mostly
consistent with experience. More consistent with experience than some of the
point systems I've seen posted as being ones used.

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
"Curevei" <cur...@aol.commetal> wrote in message
news:20020730024447...@mb-cb.aol.com...

>
> Point system is not going to be able to accurately gauge each and every
> situation. The valuations of various features of vampires is an average
> valuation for a feature. On average, out of clan disciplines, with the
> exception of Dominate and possibly Presence, are worth significantly
> less than in clan disciplines.

Sure. But this is mainly (IMO) because "clan disciplines" exist
and apply to most vampires.

Suppose we were actually allowed to "dial a vamp" to build our
crypts. In that case, any discipline combination you wanted
would be available in any combination you wanted. If you could
do that, wouldn't costing "out of clan" disciplines at a reduction
from "in clan" prices be "abusable" compared to costing all
disciplines the same?

Yes, some disciplines are certainly better than others, and some
combinations are better than others. But if all combinations
were allowed, I'd think that for practicality you'd want to price
all disciplines the same for all vampires.

In the game as it stands, where apparently *not* allowing all
possible discipline combinations in a crypt is part of the design
theory, I think you're right that "out of clan" disciplines will
generally be less usable than "in clan" ones, and maybe they
should get some price break for that. But even here in the "real
world" ;-) people do get some use out of weird non-clan discipline
combinations, especially when "out of clan" superiors are
available.

Josh
